To make a formal complaint, you should write to the Chief Executive at Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, or call 020 7188 3514, or email gstt.complaints@nhs.net. The complaint should be made within six months of the incident or one year from when you realised there was a need to complain. After lodging a complaint, they send an acknowledgement within three working days and say the investigation will be carried out by a senior member of staff; if you are still unhappy, you can ask for an independent review by the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman, but only after the Trust has investigated it.

step.detail:
Question: What does this page say about how to complain about NHS services, getting support from an NHS complaints advocate, and going to the ombudsman if unhappy? Give short verbatim quotes.
You can complain about NHS care, treatment or service, and if you need help you can get free support from an NHS complaints advocate. If you’re still unhappy after the local complaints process, you can take the complaint to the relevant ombudsman, including the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman for NHS complaints in England. The page also says complaints can be made verbally, in writing or by email.
✓ quote found in the page: ""You have the right to make a complaint about any aspect of NHS care, treatment or service, and this is written into the NHS Constitution on GOV.UK.""
✓ quote found in the page: ""If you’re making, or thinking about making, a complaint, you could get free help from an NHS complaints advocate.""
✓ quote found in the page: ""An advocate can help you to write a complaint letter and attend meetings with you, but cannot make the complaint for you or give medical or legal advice.""
✓ quote found in the page: ""If you’ve reached the end of the complaints process and are not happy with the organisation’s final decision, you have the right to bring your complaint to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman to look at.""

Question: What does this page say about how claimants should pursue clinical negligence claims against the NHS, whether they need legal advice, and whether mediation is available? Give short verbatim quotes.
The page says that if you plan to represent yourself, you need to send a “letter of claim” to the NHS Trust responsible for your care, and that if you do not have legal representation you can act “as a litigant in person.” It also says you should consider seeking independent legal advice because these claims are often complex, and it provides an Easy Read resource that “is not a replacement for legal advice.” The page does not say that mediation is available.
✓ quote found in the page: "If you do not have legal representation and you plan on representing yourself in court as a litigant in person, you will need to submit what is called a ‘letter of claim’ to the NHS Trust that was responsible for your care."
✓ quote found in the page: "Claims for clinical negligence compensation are often complex and may require expert evidence, particularly in respect to causation. We strongly recommend that you consider seeking independent legal advice to assist you in pursuing your claim."
✓ quote found in the page: "It is not a replacement for legal advice."
✓ quote found in the page: "Before making a claim it is worth considering using the NHS complaints procedure in order to find out more about what happened."

step.detail:
Question: What does this official NHS Resolution document say about time limits for bringing clinical negligence claims? Give short verbatim quotes.
The document says clinical negligence claims must generally be “issued” within three years of the date the cause of action arose or a later date of knowledge. It also says the three-year period is the “limitation period” and that, in some situations, the usual period can be modified or extended. It warns that if the incident was more than 3 years ago, you should not agree to extend it because that may waive a limitation defence.

steps.deadline: "This three year period is known as the ‘limitation period’ and it begins on the day after the cause of action (the incident causing the patient harm) arose"
points: If you act without a lawyer, NHS Resolution says you can proceed as a litigant in person.
To start, you send a letter of claim to the NHS trust responsible for your care.
NHS Resolution strongly recommends independent legal advice because these claims are complex and often need expert evidence.
The basic limitation period is 3 years from the treatment/incident or a later date of knowledge.
Using the NHS complaints procedure first can help you find out more about what happened.
requires: Identify the NHS trust responsible for the care
Usually a letter of claim before court proceedings
steps.appliesIf: A claim for damages for clinical negligence arising from NHS hospital care in England.
alternatives: Use the NHS complaints procedure first to learn more about what happened

sources.quote: If you do not have legal representation and you plan on representing yourself in court as a litigant in person, you will need to submit what is called a ‘letter of claim’ to the NHS Trust that was responsible for your care.

Claims for clinical negligence compensation are often complex and may require expert evidence, particularly in respect to causation. We strongly recommend that you consider seeking independent legal advice to assist you in pursuing your claim.
Before making a claim it is worth considering using the NHS complaints procedure in order to find out more about what happened.
i) The date the cause of action arose (e.g. the date of the consultation or treatment during which complications arose); or
ii) A later date of knowledge (i.e. the date from which the patient first became aware that they may have suffered an injury as a result of negligent treatment)
This three year period is known as the ‘limitation period’ and it begins on the day after the cause of action (the incident causing the patient harm) arose

steps.what: For an adult missed-fracture clinical negligence claim, the official legal-aid scope I found is extremely narrow and appears aimed at severe neurological injury cases meeting special conditions, not ordinary adult injury claims. The official routes I found are the public legal-aid checker for eligibility and, outside legal aid, conditional fee agreements ('no win, no fee') with a success-fee cap.
points: The public legal-aid page says to use the online checker to see if you can get legal aid and how to apply.

The clinical-negligence scope in legislation is for civil legal services for a claim for damages where clinical negligence caused a neurological injury and the individual is severely disabled, subject to conditions.
That means this adult wrist-fracture claim does not obviously fit the ordinary legal-aid scope found in this run.

sources.quote: If you do not have legal representation and you plan on representing yourself in court as a litigant in person, you will need to submit what is called a ‘letter of claim’ to the NHS Trust that was responsible for your care.

Claims for clinical negligence compensation are often complex and may require expert evidence, particularly in respect to causation. We strongly recommend that you consider seeking independent legal advice to assist you in pursuing your claim.
Before making a claim it is worth considering using the NHS complaints procedure in order to find out more about what happened.

The basic rule is that claims for damages arising from clinical negligence must be
formal
ly “issued”
within three years
of either:

A later date of knowledge (i.e. the date from which the patient first became
aware that they
may have suffered an injury as a result of negligent treatment)

This three year period is known as the ‘limitation period’ and it begins on the day
after the cause of action (the incident causing the patient harm) arose

steps.what: For an adult missed-fracture clinical negligence claim, the official legal-aid scope I found is extremely narrow and appears aimed at severe neurological injury cases meeting special conditions, not ordinary adult injury claims. The official routes I found are the public legal-aid checker for eligibility and, outside legal aid, conditional fee agreements ('no win, no fee') with a success-fee cap.
points: The public legal-aid page says to use the online checker to see if you can get legal aid and how to apply.

The clinical-negligence scope in legislation is for civil legal services for a claim for damages where clinical negligence caused a neurological injury and the individual is severely disabled, subject to conditions.
That means this adult wrist-fracture claim does not obviously fit the ordinary legal-aid scope found in this run.
Conditional fee agreement success fees in personal injury claims are capped at 25% of damages excluding future care and future loss, and the cap includes VAT.
You can also use the official legal-aid adviser finder for clinical negligence.
steps.appliesIf: Legal aid only if the clinical-negligence case fits the narrow statutory scope; otherwise private funding such as a CFA may be needed.
missing: Whether the injury involved severe neurological disability within the statutory category
Household finances if legal aid were potentially in scope
Whether a solicitor is willing to offer a CFA

sources.quote: Use the ‘Check if you can get legal aid’ service to check your eligibility and find out how to apply.
Search for official legal aid advisers in England and Wales.

Civil legal services provided in relation to a claim for damages in respect of clinical negligence which caused a neurological injury to an individual (“V”) as a result of which V is severely disabled, but only where the first and second conditions are met.

Article 5 provides that, in order to be enforceable, a CFA must not provide for a success fee which, including VAT, is greater than 25% of the damages awarded to the claimant for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and damages for pecuniary loss (save for future pecuniary loss),
The cap will be set at 25% of the damages other than those for future care and loss.

steps.body: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust
steps.what: St Thomas' Hospital is part of Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, so an NHS complaint about this A&E care goes to the trust. A reachable official trust-family complaints page says formal complaints can be sent to the Chief Executive, and the trust's own online complaint form was found at https://www.guysandstthomas.nhs.uk/form/complaints-form but blocked the automated browser in this run.
steps.deadline: "it should be made within six months of the incident or one year from when you realised that there was a need to complain."
steps.wall: bot_check on the trust complaint form and trust complaint page in this run
points: St Thomas' is under Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust.
A formal complaint should usually be made within 6 months of the incident or 1 year from when you realised there was a need to complain.
The trust says it will acknowledge the complaint within 3 working days.
The investigation is carried out by a senior member of staff.
PALS is an alternative early route for concerns before or alongside a formal complaint.
steps.appliesIf: NHS/public care at St Thomas' Hospital.
missing: Whether you have already complained to the trust or PALS
Date of any trust complaint response

points: You must complain to the organisation first.

There are large-print and Easy Read complaint forms as alternatives to the online route.
requires: A complaint to Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust first
Usually the organisation's final response or the end of the local complaints process
steps.appliesIf: NHS complaints in England after the provider complaint process has been used.
missing: Whether the trust has sent its final complaint response

steps.what: For an adult missed-fracture clinical negligence claim, the official legal-aid scope I found is extremely narrow and appears aimed at severe neurological injury cases meeting special conditions, not ordinary adult injury claims. The official routes I found are the public legal-aid checker for eligibility and, outside legal aid, conditional fee agreements ('no win, no fee') with a success-fee cap.
points: The public legal-aid page says to use the online checker to see if you can get legal aid and how to apply.

The clinical-negligence scope in legislation is for civil legal services for a claim for damages where clinical negligence caused a neurological injury and the individual is severely disabled, subject to conditions.
That means this adult wrist-fracture claim does not obviously fit the ordinary legal-aid scope found in this run.
Conditional fee agreement success fees in personal injury claims are capped at 25% of damages excluding future care and future loss, and the cap includes VAT.
You can also use the official legal-aid adviser finder for clinical negligence.
steps.appliesIf: Legal aid only if the clinical-negligence case fits the narrow statutory scope; otherwise private funding such as a CFA may be needed.

The cap will be set at 25% of the damages other than those for future care and loss.

thoughts.detail: {"summary":"St Thomas’ Hospital is NHS care under Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust. For a complaint, the trust route is first; the reachable official trust-family page says complain within 6 months of the incident or 1 year from when you realised there was a need to complain, and they should acknowledge within 3 working days. If you are still unhappy after the trust process, the independent next step is the Public Service Ombudsman, usually within 12 months of knowing about the issue; for compensation, the official route I found is a clinical negligence claim, usually started by a letter of claim, with a general 3-year limitation period, and ordinary adult legal aid does not obviously cover this kind of case."}

Core facts are now sourced from reachable official pages; start recording the routes and note the two blocked trust pages as walls.

Complain: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust. St Thomas' Hospital is part of Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, so an NHS complaint about this A&E care goes to the trust. A reachable official trust-family complaints page says formal complaints can be sent to the Chief Executive, and the trust's own online complaint form was found at https://www.guysandstthomas.nhs.uk/form/complaints-form but blocked the automated browser in this run.

If that fails: Public Service Ombudsman. If the trust's complaint answer is not good enough, the independent next step is the Public Service Ombudsman for NHS complaints in England. You must complain to the trust first, then use the Ombudsman's complaint checker and form. (one official source)

Compensation: NHS Resolution. The compensation route I found for harm from NHS care here is a clinical negligence claim against the trust, usually started with a letter of claim and, if needed, pursued in court. In this run I did not find a current official England no-fault or redress application route for ordinary hospital negligence; the official route I found is the negligence claim route below. (one official source)

Paying for help: GOV.UK / Legal Aid Agency. For an adult missed-fracture clinical negligence claim, the official legal-aid scope I found is extremely narrow and appears aimed at severe neurological injury cases meeting special conditions, not ordinary adult injury claims. The official routes I found are the public legal-aid checker for eligibility and, outside legal aid, conditional fee agreements ('no win, no fee') with a success-fee cap.

says.detail:
uksiem_20130689_en.pdf (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2013/689/pdfs/uksiem_20130689_en.pdf)
The page says the cap is “greater than 25% of the damages awarded to the claimant for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and damages for pecuniary loss (save for future pecuniary loss),” and that it is “including VAT.” It also says the cap protects “future care and loss,” and that the Government said the cap “will be set at 25% of the damages other than those for future care and loss.”
Quotes: "Article 5 provides that, in order to be enforceable, a CFA must not provide for a success fee which, including VAT, is greater than 25% of the damages awarded to the claimant for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and damages for pecuniary loss (save for future pecuniary loss)," | "The cap will be set at 25% of the damages other than those for future care and loss." | "The 25% cap is intended to protect claimants' damages, specifically those relating to future care and loss," | "The cap will be set at 25% of the damages other than those for future care and loss."

says.text: Compensation: NHS Resolution. The compensation route I found for harm from NHS care here is a clinical negligence claim against the trust, usually started with a letter of claim and, if needed, pursued in court. In this run I did not find a current official England no-fault or redress application route for ordinary hospital negligence; the official route I found is the negligence claim route below. (one official source)

Paying for help: GOV.UK / Legal Aid Agency. For an adult missed-fracture clinical negligence claim, the official legal-aid scope I found is extremely narrow and appears aimed at severe neurological injury cases meeting special conditions, not ordinary adult injury claims. The official routes I found are the public legal-aid checker for eligibility and, outside legal aid, conditional fee agreements ('no win, no fee') with a success-fee cap.

Finding a lawyer: The Law Society. The official profession-run directory I found is the Law Society's Find a Solicitor service. You can use it to search for solicitors in England and Wales who do clinical negligence work and then narrow by location such as London. (one official source)

Clinical guidance: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). The national body I found publishing the main evidence-based clinical guidance for NHS care in England is NICE. Trust clinicians may also use local policies, but NICE is the official national guidance body shown in this run. (one official source)

Free help: NHS England / AvMA. For complaints, NHS England says you can get free help from an NHS complaints advocate. For independent support about avoidable medical harm more broadly, AvMA offers free independent advice, support and information.

Your records: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust. The reachable official records route I found is through the trust-family Royal Brompton & Harefield pages, which point back to Guy's and St Thomas' records pages and give the subject-access contact details at St Thomas' Hospital. The trust's own records pages on guysandstthomas.nhs.uk blocked the automated browser in this run, but the reachable pages say to use an access-to-records form and send it by post or email. (one official source)

St Thomas’ Hospital is NHS care under Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust. For a complaint, the trust route is first; the reachable official trust-family page says complain within 6 months of the incident or 1 year from when you realised there was a need to complain, and they should acknowledge within 3 working days. If you are still unhappy after the trust process, the independent next step is the Public Service Ombudsman, usually within 12 months of knowing about the issue; for compensation, the official route I found is a clinical negligence claim, usually started by a letter of claim, with a general 3-year limitation period, and ordinary adult legal aid does not obviously cover this kind of case.

Question: What does this official page say about how to make a formal complaint, any deadline, stages, and response times? Give short verbatim quotes.
To make a formal complaint, you should write to the Chief Executive at Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, or call 020 7188 3514, or email gstt.complaints@nhs.net.
